description: This case study reflects on how Baltimore planned for the resilience of its food system to disasters, at a time when few US cities had considered food in disaster planning. An academic centre, the Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future, partnered with the city's Department of Planning. First, an Emergency Food Working Group met three times over three months and produced an emergency food access protocol for acute events such as storms. Then the partners wrote the Baltimore Food System Resilience Advisory Report from 36 key-informant interviews with food system stakeholders, a literature review and GIS mapping; it assessed the food system's vulnerability to hazards and how prepared businesses and agencies were for supply disruptions, and it set out policy recommendations and a framework for thinking about food system vulnerabilities. The article is free to read and download as a PDF from the open access Journal of Agriculture, Food Systems, and Community Development (2018). Coverage is Baltimore City. Caveats: a reflective participant-observer account; the article page shows only a copyright notice, not a licence. Simulation uses: stakeholder-derived vulnerabilities and response protocols to parameterise urban food supply disruption scenarios. Related records: Toronto's food system climate vulnerability assessment (case_study-toronto-food-system-climate-vulnerability-assessment) is a comparable city study, and the USDA Food Access Research Atlas (data-usda-ers-food-access-research-atlas) maps baseline food access.
